## Vision and core hypothesis

Amarna Letters is a strategy game with no diplomacy rules: the engine enforces physics, and every treaty, alliance and betrayal is invented by the players. It is set among the seven Great Kings of the Late Bronze Age, whose clay-tablet correspondence (c. 1360–1332 BCE) shows diplomacy at its rawest: disputed status, gold of doubtful purity, detained messengers and promises nobody could verify.

**Core hypothesis.** If communication is delayed, carried by people with their own motives and impossible to verify fully, then norms of trust, reputation and enforcement will emerge on their own. That emergence is the game.

**What changes compared with Diplomacy.** In Diplomacy you talk *to* the other player, instantly and unfiltered. In Amarna Letters you talk *through* someone: every message is delayed, interpreted and possibly bought, so the channel itself becomes a battlefield. On top of that come an economy, written evidence and forgery, characters with hidden agency, asymmetric powers and hidden information.

**Target experience.** Players read people, not dice. Uncertainty always has a face and a motive the player can reason about.

**Why now.** A table could never run this game: it needs a game master playing twenty characters at once, keeping secrets and tracking who knows what. A deterministic engine plus small language models can fill that role today.
